name: Toungoo Dynasty (Burma)
summary: The ruling dynasty of Burma from 1510 to 1752. Under Bayinnaung it built probably the largest empire in the history of Southeast Asia.

location.value: Burma (Myanmar), at its peak from Manipur to Laos and Siam.

terrain.value: The Irrawaddy and Sittaung river valleys, surrounded by hills and mountains.

climate.value: Monsoon, with heavy rain on the coast and a dry central zone.

resources.value: Rice, teak, rubies and other gems, and Indian Ocean ports.

disasters.value: Famines during long wars, such as in the 1590s.

population.value: No reliable estimate; perhaps a few million.

urbanisation.value: Pegu (Bago) was a great port city in the 16th century.

migration.value: War captives from Siam, Laos and Manipur were resettled in Burma.

economicBase.value: Rice farming in the dry zone and delta; sea trade through Pegu.

tradeRoutes.value: Indian Ocean trade through Pegu and Syriam with India, Portugal and the Malay world.

wealth.value: No estimate is possible for this period.

moneyAndTax.value: Silver and lead used by weight; taxes on land and trade.

inequality.value: The king and nobles controlled land and labour.

governmentType.value: An absolute monarchy based on Buddhist kingship.

keyRulers.value: Tabinshwehti and Bayinnaung (1550–1581), who reunified the lands of the Pagan Kingdom.

succession.value: Hereditary, but often violent, with princes fighting for the throne.

institutions.value: Reformed administration in the Nyaungyan restoration.

stability.value: The First Toungoo Empire collapsed in 1599; the Nyaungyan restoration followed.

eliteConflict.value: Rival princes and governors rebelled after strong kings died.

armyAndTech.value: Large armies with Portuguese mercenaries and firearms.

majorWars.value: Wars with Ayutthaya (1564, 1569) and Lan Xang.

territoryChange.value: Probably the largest empire in Southeast Asian history under Bayinnaung.

alliancesRivals.value: Rivals included Ayutthaya, Lan Xang, Manipur and the Arakan kingdom.

inventions.value: Little is known; Portuguese guns and gunners were used.

scienceEducation.value: Monastic schools taught boys to read.

openness.value: Hired Portuguese soldiers and traded with Europeans.

communicationTransport.value: Boats on the Irrawaddy and Sittaung; sea ports such as Syriam.

religion.value: Theravada Buddhism; kings built and restored many pagodas.

languageWriting.value: Burmese, written in its own script; Pali for religious texts.

artsArchitecture.value: The Kanbawzathadi Palace at Pegu and the Shwemawdaw Pagoda.

socialStructure.value: King, nobles, commoners and slaves; many people owed service to the crown.

sharedIdentity.value: Buddhist kingship united Burmese, Mon and Shan subjects.

dailyLife.value: Wooden houses on stilts; rice, fish paste (ngapi) and vegetables.

neighbours.value: Ayutthaya, Lan Xang, Mughal India, Arakan and Ming China.

ideasReligions.value: Spread Theravada Buddhism and Buddhist kingship.

colonisation.value: None overseas; expanded on land across mainland Southeast Asia.

riseSignals.value: Founded in 1510 in the small state of Toungoo.
riseSignals.source: Wikipedia: Toungoo dynasty (checked 6 Nov 2026); Lieberman, Strange Parallels vol. 1 (2003)

peakPeriod.value: Under Bayinnaung (1550–1581), whose empire was the largest in Southeast Asian history.
peakPeriod.source: Wikipedia: Toungoo dynasty (checked 6 Nov 2026); Lieberman, Strange Parallels vol. 1 (2003)

declineSignals.value: Overstretch after Bayinnaung; revolts and collapse in 1599, then a weaker restored kingdom.

outcome.value: Fell to the Mon in 1752; the Konbaung dynasty followed.
outcome.source: Wikipedia: Toungoo dynasty (checked 6 Nov 2026); Lieberman, Strange Parallels vol. 1 (2003)

sources.value: Burmese chronicles. Checked against Wikipedia (“Toungoo dynasty”).
